questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The permanent seats created in 1945
questions.learningObjective: identify the checkable feature that explains the 1945 design of the main council
questions.stem: The organisation set up in 1945 named five states as permanent members of its main council, gave each of them a second-vote power in a written charter, and made the charter enter into force only once those five had signed it. Which feature of that package most directly explains the shape it took?

options.text: The five had supplied the largest contingents and all of the funding
options.misconception: credits military and financial contribution as the reason for the second vote

options.text: The five made the second vote a condition of joining the organisation at all
options.misconception: treats membership as conditional on holding the named second-vote power

options.text: The organisation came into legal existence only when those five ratified it
The five reserved the right to appoint the organisation's paid staff
options.misconception: confuses a blocking power on decisions with control over appointments

questions.explanation: The charter's own entry-into-force clause tied the organisation's legal existence to ratification by the five named states, so those states could not be outvoted by numbers and had nothing to gain from withdrawing. That is a checkable feature of the text rather than a guess about intent. The other answers explain the arrangement through contributions, a membership bargain, or staff appointments, none of which is what the clause does.
questions.hint: Ask what the charter itself says had to happen before the organisation legally existed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a blocking power works
questions.learningObjective: describe the operative effect of a permanent member's negative vote
questions.stem: Under the 1945 charter, a state outside the five permanent members that wanted the organisation to act had to win a vote in the main council on which none of the five voted no. Which feature of the rule explains that outcome most directly?

options.text: Only members on the council were allowed to call a vote on a threat
options.misconception: invents a rule that restricts who may put a question to the council

options.text: A single negative vote by a permanent member was enough to defeat it
The sponsoring states had to vote in favour before debate could even open
options.misconception: assumes a sponsorship threshold for taking up a question

options.text: The general assembly could reverse such a defeat by a large majority
options.misconception: believes the assembly can overturn a defeat in the council

questions.explanation: The charter required, for decisions on non-procedural questions, concurring votes including no negative vote by a permanent member, so a single state could stop a resolution that every other member wanted. That is the whole of the mechanism, and it is written into the text. The distractors each add a rule the charter does not contain: a restriction on who may raise a question, a sponsorship threshold, and an assembly override that would make the negative vote pointless.
questions.hint: Count how many states would have to agree before a decision goes through.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The founding text on threats to the peace
questions.learningObjective: separate a reporting procedure from a grant of coercive power
questions.stem: A modern summary of the 1945 charter's provisions on threats to the peace says that a state believing another is endangering peace should bring the matter to the main council, that the council then decides whether the situation does endanger peace, and that the charter does not itself authorise any army to be sent. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

options.text: A route for getting a threat before the council, without a force standing behind it
A general licence for any member to send troops once a threat was agreed
options.misconception: reads a reporting procedure as authority to use military force

options.text: A power for a standing military committee to act without reconvening
options.misconception: invents a war-declaring power that the text does not create

options.text: An agreement that sanctions would follow automatically from a vote
options.misconception: credits a binding enforcement clause the summary does not mention

questions.explanation: The summary is careful to separate two steps: a state may raise the matter, and the council then finds whether peace is endangered. It says nothing about who acts afterwards, and it expressly denies that the text authorises an army. So the text establishes a procedure, not a force and not a licence. Each distractor adds a step the summary does not contain, which is the standard way a summary gets read past.
questions.hint: Count the steps the summary actually describes before anyone acts.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the design entrenched the division
questions.learningObjective: explain why sponsors abstained rather than using their blocking power
questions.stem: After 1945 the five permanent members frequently left the council chamber without voting rather than recording a negative vote, and the body seldom took action in a dispute between one of them and another government. Which feature of the rule produces that pattern?

options.text: A permanent member could stop a decision by not taking part at all
The charter let the general assembly overturn any council decision
options.misconception: invents an assembly override that would make blocking pointless

options.text: Only the general assembly could decide a matter was a threat
options.misconception: moves the identifying power out of the council and into the assembly

options.text: The five had to agree unanimously before any threat was discussed
options.misconception: turns the sponsors' unanimity into a rule barring discussion

questions.explanation: Because a decision needed no negative vote from the five, a permanent member that wanted to stop action did not have to be recorded voting no, which would have been a visible and costly act, and could simply be absent. That is the mechanical reason the council's action dried up in disputes involving a sponsor. The other options propose a rule that either would have removed the need for abstention or would have made the whole design inoperative.
questions.hint: Ask what happened if a sponsor was in the room but said nothing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the bargain was accepted
questions.learningObjective: infer what states accepted in exchange for a design they could not control
questions.stem: Fifty-one governments signed the 1945 charter even though five of them could prevent any decision the other forty-six might want, and several of those signatories had fought alongside those five in the same war. What does that acceptance indicate about the bargain those states struck?

options.text: A guarantee against another great-power war, bought at the cost of power over the sponsors
A wish for an organisation able to impose its decisions on all states equally
options.misconception: reads the design as equal power rather than as a trade

options.text: An expectation that the five would be isolated whenever they blocked a vote
options.misconception: invents an enforcement mechanism the design does not contain

options.text: An intention to use the charter as the legal basis for ending colonial rule
options.misconception: attributes a decolonisation purpose to the founding bargain

questions.explanation: The signatories' recorded fear was another war among the great powers, and the only body able to act against one of them was one the five could veto, so the signatory accepting an inability to act against a sponsor was the price of an organisation that could be aimed at anyone. The evidence is the coincidence of co-operation in the war with acceptance of a design that excluded them. The distractors claim a power the signatories did not gain, a punishment they had no mechanism for, or a purpose that belongs to a later decade.
questions.hint: Ask what the signatories wanted prevented, and who the new body could reach.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which a frozen council was bypassed
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps by which action was taken without a blocking power
questions.stem: A war began in Asia in 1950 and a member state reported an armed attack on another to the main council. Put these four developments in the order in which they happened.

options.text: A government that was a permanent member of the council was absent and could not be reached
The government of the attacked state sent a letter to the council describing the attack
The council adopted resolutions calling on members to help and barring aid to the attacker
Several members sent contingents that served under one combined command

questions.explanation: The report came first, because the council had nothing to consider until a state put the matter before it, and the absence of a permanent member mattered only after the letter arrived, since it was the reason no negative vote could be cast. Only then could the council vote to call for help and to close the organisation's members off from assisting the attacker, and only after those resolutions did contingents move to a single combined command. Reversing the first two steps loses the causal link, since an absent member cannot unblock a question nobody has asked.
questions.hint: A council can only be blocked on a question once the question has been put to it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A proxy conflict organised through a membership body
questions.learningObjective: explain how a coalition war produced a formalised alignment
questions.stem: A war in Asia from 1950 to 1953 was fought by troops from a coalition of member states under one headquarters, with ships and aircraft supplied by members from other regions, and it ended in an armistice that left the front line where it had begun. Which later development does that experience best explain?

options.text: A multilateral defence treaty signed by one side, and a rival pact formed soon after
A standing claim by the organisation to station troops in any member state
options.misconception: invents a general right of stationing troops that no text created

options.text: A change in the charter naming the attackers as the organisation's target
options.misconception: claims the founding text was rewritten to name a state

options.text: A decision by the members to abandon written alliances for the rest of the decade
options.misconception: reports the opposite of what followed the war

questions.explanation: The war showed that a coalition could fight successfully and that an armistice could hold a front line without settling anything, and the visible result afterwards was the formalisation of blocs in signed defence treaties, with each side's list of members published for the other to read. The checkable feature is the sequence of treaty signatures, not the arguments about the war. The other answers claim a charter amendment, a general right of stationing troops, and the abandonment of alliances, all of which run against the record.
questions.hint: Ask what was signed afterwards, and by whom.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The features of a bloc built against another
questions.learningObjective: select the structural features of a mutual defence arrangement
questions.stem: Two rival regional alliances were created in the mid-1950s, each with a signed treaty, a standing command structure, and a published membership list that the other side read closely. Which features belong to the structure of such an arrangement? Select all that apply.

options.text: A written treaty each signer's government could invoke against a stated kind of act
A standing command structure allowing joint planning before any fighting started
A shared currency that settled trade disputes between the two blocs
options.misconception: invents a monetary arrangement for a military pact

options.text: A rule that every ally of a signer was obliged to join automatically
options.misconception: assumes membership extended to allies by automatic right

questions.explanation: A defence arrangement needs a document that states what a signer's government must do when a defined act occurs, and it needs a command that can plan before a crisis, otherwise the first days of any war would be spent inventing a chain of command. Currency settlement and automatic membership for allies belong to no such treaty, and the second is a claim about obligations that alliances have historically refused, because it would hand the choice to a third party.
questions.hint: Ask what has to exist before a crisis, and what a treaty must state to be usable.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A year of applications
questions.learningObjective: read an official record for the reason behind a transfer of power
questions.stem: In the course of one year an imperial cabinet approved self-government for a series of territories, several of which had asked for it at nearly the same moment, and the ministers' own minutes recorded that the decision rested on the point that holding them any longer had become too expensive. Which reading of that record is right?

options.text: The timing came from the imperial government's costs, and the demands supplied the occasion
The empire had already judged every one of those territories to be ready
options.misconception: treats the assessed readiness as the reason the record gives

options.text: The applications were granted to honour promises of a date made years before
options.misconception: invents a prior written promise the record does not mention

options.text: The territories had already become independent before self-government was approved
options.misconception: confuses self-government with independence

questions.explanation: The minutes name cost, not readiness, and they place the decision in the imperial cabinet rather than in the territories, so the sequence is that several demands arrived together, which let the government pick a moment when the expense of continuing to hold them was highest. The other readings substitute a competence judgement, an unrecorded promise, and a change of status the record does not describe.
questions.hint: Ask whose reasons the record gives, and who was taking the decision.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A circular that set the timetable
questions.learningObjective: analyse who set the conditions for self-government
questions.stem: In the early 1960s a colonial office circular instructed governors to offer self-government wherever a territory showed a representative majority, a written constitution, and a civil service whose senior officers were local, and it attached the list of territories meeting all three tests. Which feature of that instruction does the most work?

options.text: The conditions were written in the imperial capital, so a local demand had to fit a checklist
The circular set a single fixed date by which every territory must qualify
options.misconception: converts a checklist of three tests into a published schedule

options.text: The circular ended the governor's authority over each territory it listed
options.misconception: infers an immediate transfer of power from a statement of readiness

options.text: The circular asked territories to reject written constitutions until maturity was proved
options.misconception: reverses the stated conditions and invents a delay rule

questions.explanation: The circular put the test in the imperial government's hands: the three conditions were named in advance, and a territory's own claim counted only once it matched them, so the order of decisions is that the framework existed first and local demands were measured against it. The other options read a checklist as a calendar, as an immediate transfer, or as a rule against constitutions, none of which follows from an instruction about when to offer self-government.
questions.hint: Ask who wrote the three tests, and where they were written.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Borders drawn before a colony existed
questions.learningObjective: explain a problem created by a boundary drawn on a map
questions.stem: A state that has just become independent has a straight northern edge, a straight western edge, a river in the south, and several large communities whose main settlements lie in neighbouring countries. Which feature of that situation does the most to create trouble inside the new state?

options.text: The edges follow lines drawn by outsiders, so communities were joined and split administratively
Only the river edge can be revised later, since the others are straight
options.misconception: confines the problem to a natural boundary that is no easier to change

options.text: The state is too small to administer several languages in government
options.misconception: reduces a boundary problem to language administration

options.text: The neighbours have borders of their own, so nothing can be claimed as internal
options.misconception: invents an absence of neighbours to block the analysis

questions.explanation: When boundaries are drawn on a map without asking who lives where, the resulting state inherits communities cut through and others joined to strangers, and every one of them is a claim on the new government for access to land, jobs, or a vote. The other answers treat the straight lines as if their geometry were the issue, or move the problem into language administration or into the neighbours' conduct, none of which is what the inherited lines themselves create.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a community that ends up on both sides of a line.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The contest for the centre
questions.learningObjective: explain why an army becomes the final arbiter of political outcomes
questions.stem: In a new state with several regions and a long frontier next to powerful neighbours, the army has repeatedly stepped in after elections to settle who actually holds office. Which feature of the situation best explains that recurring role?

options.text: The army holds the coercive force while elections decide only who commands it
The constitution names the army as a court of appeal for political disputes
options.misconception: claims a written constitutional power for the army that the record lacks

options.text: The army is paid in foreign currency, so no elected government can replace it
options.misconception: turns a funding arrangement into a constitutional bar to removal

options.text: Only one region may vote, so the army merely follows the recorded majority
options.misconception: invents a restricted franchise to explain a political intervention

questions.explanation: A contest that determines only who commands the coercive force is a contest over the state itself, so an army that has acted as referee once has a reason to act again, because a result it dislikes is a threat to its own position. questions.hint: Ask what an election in such a state actually decides, and who holds the force that decides it.

questions.topic: A third option in choosing alliances
questions.learningObjective: state what non-alignment required of a new government
questions.stem: A 1955 conference of governments from Asia and Africa, most of them newly independent, produced a declaration refusing membership of a great-power military alliance and refusing the use of national territory for such an alliance's forces. Which feature of that position is the substantive one?

options.text: It fixed which alliances and foreign bases a government must refuse, leaving the rest open
It promised each participant military help from the great powers themselves
options.misconception: invents a protection guarantee that the declaration refuses to seek

options.text: It was the first step toward forming a third alliance of its own
options.misconception: reads a refusal to join blocs as the creation of a new one

options.text: It required every participant to dissolve its own armed forces
options.misconception: invents a demilitarisation condition the declaration does not set

It creates no new army, no new alliance and no disarmament, and the distractor that treats it as the embryo of a third bloc misses the point of refusing blocs in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask what the declaration lists, and what it deliberately does not create.

questions.topic: A declaration that refused the blocs
questions.learningObjective: read a declaration for the specific commitments it makes
questions.stem: A modern summary of the 1955 conference's closing declaration lists ten points, which include that participants should not join a military alliance directed against another power, should not permit its bases on their territory, should not intervene in another's internal affairs, and should settle disputes among themselves peacefully. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

options.text: A defined set of refusals, leaving each government free on questions not listed
A permanent ban on any defence agreement whatever its form or purpose
options.misconception: extends a refusal aimed at one arrangement into a total prohibition

options.text: A new body with authority to settle disputes among the signatories
options.misconception: invents an institution that the summary nowhere creates

options.text: A transfer of colonial territories to their inhabitants by signed agreement
options.misconception: reads a document of self-restraint as a transfer of sovereignty

questions.hint: Check whether any of the ten points covers a case the summary does not list.

questions.topic: Writing down how a new state is organised
questions.learningObjective: identify the feature of a federal constitution that holds a diverse state together
questions.stem: A new state adopted a written constitution that divided authority between a centre and units with their own enumerated lists of powers, made the constitution unalterable except by the stated procedure, and gave a court the power to rule in a conflict between the two levels. Which feature of that design does most to hold a large and varied state together?

options.text: Each level holds defined powers and a court can settle a dispute between them
The text was adopted by referendum, so no future government can change it
options.misconception: assumes a ratification route makes amendment impossible

options.text: The centre was given every power and the units were left no list of their own
options.misconception: describes a unitary state and calls its constitution federal

options.text: The judges were appointed for life, so the court can refuse any elected government
options.misconception: promotes a safeguard about appointments into an independence guarantee

questions.explanation: A design holds a large state together when neither level can take the other's field, and enumerated lists plus a court ruling are the two features that deliver that: the units keep something the centre cannot absorb, and the centre has a way to settle the argument without a fight. The other three each claim a stronger and less plausible effect, from unchangeable text to judges who can refuse any government.
questions.hint: Ask what stops the centre from simply taking over a unit's field.

questions.topic: Redrawing internal boundaries
questions.learningObjective: explain the problem a linguistic reorganisation was meant to reduce
questions.stem: A few years after independence one state reorganised its internal units so that each grouped together people who shared a language, and the reorganisation was enacted by parliament over local objections rather than left to each region. Which problem was that measure most directly built to reduce?

The cost of building roads across regions of very different sizes
options.misconception: reduces a political settlement to an infrastructure budget

options.text: Pressure from neighbours to redraw the country's outer boundary
options.misconception: misdirects an internal reorganisation into an external demand

options.text: The lack of any written constitution for the new units themselves
options.misconception: recasts a boundary measure as a constitutional measure

questions.topic: The institutions of a regional project
questions.learningObjective: identify the institutional feature that matters in a dispute between members
questions.stem: A regional project created in 1975 set up a supreme authority made up of the members' heads of government, a permanent secretariat staffed by its own civil servants and based in one member, a legislature whose members were drawn from national parliaments, and a court for disputes between members. Which feature would matter most when two members fall out with each other?

options.text: A standing court with an appointed membership, since a case does not need both governments' consent
The legislature of national parliamentarians, which can expel a member at any time
options.misconception: invents a legislative sanction no such institution carries

options.text: The secretariat, which can order a member to pay compensation out of its budget
options.misconception: promotes an administrative office into a court of awards

options.text: The heads of government, who can settle any dispute they choose before a case is filed
options.misconception: treats political preference as a legal bar to proceedings

questions.topic: A regional treaty's text
questions.learningObjective: read a treaty's provisions for what a dated obligation commits
questions.stem: A modern summary of a regional treaty concluded in 1975 records that members agreed to free the movement of their citizens after a nine-year transition, to remove internal tariffs over the same period, to refer disputes between themselves to a court, and to keep the organisation's institutions staffed by its own civil servants. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

A right to withdraw from any article at any point during the transition
options.misconception: converts a transition timetable into a general exit right

options.text: A court whose rulings are advisory because the members are sovereign
options.misconception: turns a named court into an advisory body it was not made to be

options.misconception: redirects internal liberalization into a customs union with outsiders

The founding statement was amended to remove the non-interference principle entirely

questions.topic: A permanent seat after a superpower dissolved
questions.learningObjective: explain what a permanent seat remained attached to
questions.stem: When one of the five permanent members of the main council ceased to exist in 1991, the government of the state claiming to continue it wrote to the organisation asserting that it had taken over the membership and the seat, and the seat was used without interruption afterwards. Which feature of that succession is the important one?

options.text: The seat was treated as attached to the permanent membership, so it survived the state
The seat was reallocated to another member selected by a vote of the council
options.misconception: claims the seat was handed to a different member instead of held

options.text: The seat stood empty until the question of succession had been settled
options.misconception: claims a suspension that never took effect in practice

options.text: The charter was amended so that the council had six permanent members
options.misconception: claims the founding text was rewritten to enlarge the permanent five

questions.explanation: A permanent seat is a status conferred by the charter on a named state, so what a successor had to establish was that it was the same membership in law and not a new applicant, and the uninterrupted use of the seat shows the other members accepted that framing. The distractors report a reallocation, a vacancy, or an amendment, each of which would have required a decision the record does not show being taken.
questions.hint: Ask what the seat was an attribute of, and what a successor had to show.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the end of a superpower did not change
questions.learningObjective: identify the limit on reform of the council's composition
questions.stem: The dissolution of one permanent member in 1991 left a single great power standing, and for years afterwards governments argued that the council's permanent membership no longer matched the distribution of power in the world. Which statement about that argument is correct?

options.text: The charter names the permanent members, so no change was possible without a ratified amendment
A majority vote in the council could have altered its own composition directly
options.misconception: believes the council may amend its founding text by majority

options.text: The seat lapsed by itself when the state holding it ceased to exist
options.misconception: repeats the claim that the seat fell vacant, which the practice denied

options.text: The general assembly settled the question with a decision of binding effect
options.misconception: invents an assembly ruling with legal force over the charter

questions.explanation: The argument about mismatch is a claim about power, and the reply to it is a claim about law: the charter fixes the permanent members, so any enlargement needs the amendment procedure and the ratifications it prescribes, which is why the mismatch could be argued about indefinitely without the composition changing. The distractors each supply a mechanism the charter does not contain, and would each settle the question in a way that never happened.
questions.hint: Ask what would have been legally required, not what would have been desirable.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A letter about continuity
questions.learningObjective: read a diplomatic note for the kind of claim it makes
questions.stem: A modern summary of a note sent in December 1991 by the government of the state that had dissolved the one occupying a permanent seat says that the sending state continues the dissolved state's membership, intends to preserve its responsibilities, and asks that its participation in the council and in the other organs continue without interruption. The admission of a new member, completed by a decision of the general assembly
options.misconception: reads a unilateral notification as a finished admission

options.text: An agreed transfer of the seat to a different member chosen by the council
options.misconception: converts a claim into an allocation to another member

options.text: A final renunciation of the seat while a future arrangement was prepared
options.misconception: reverses the request, which was for continuation not for release

questions.explanation: The note is a claim, not a grant: it asserts continuity on the ground of inherited responsibility and asks the organisation to act accordingly, which means the summary establishes what the sender asserted and what it requested, not that the request was approved. questions.hint: Ask what the sender asserts and requests, as against what anyone granted.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutional vacuum of a transition
questions.learningObjective: explain what an institutional vacuum is and how it gets filled
questions.stem: A state replacing a communist one had no settled body able to say which of its two chief institutions was supreme, so in 1993 the president issued a decree dissolving the elected legislature, troops surrounded its building, and a constitution adopted weeks later left the presidency clearly the stronger. Which feature makes that an institutional vacuum?

options.text: Neither institution's authority was settled, so a contest of force filled the gap
A court had already dissolved the legislature lawfully before the decree was signed
options.misconception: invents a judicial step that came before the decree

options.text: The new constitution deliberately left the two institutions equal in every field
options.misconception: misreads a text that settled the question in favour of one side

options.text: The army had been given a permanent seat inside the legislature beforehand
options.misconception: turns troops around a building into a formal institutional power

questions.explanation: An institutional vacuum is a gap where a rule about who decides is missing, so that anyone can fill it by acting first, and the sequence of decree, troops, and a constitution written afterwards is the textbook sequence: the contest settles the question and the text records it. The distractors each supply a legal step, a balanced constitution, or a formal military power that would have made the contest unnecessary, and none is in the record.
questions.hint: Ask what rule was missing, and which came first, the contest or the constitution.

questions.topic: A settlement written after the contest
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a settlement reached by force from one reached by procedure
questions.stem: In 1993 troops surrounded a legislature, a decree dissolved it, and a constitution adopted shortly afterwards left the presidency clearly stronger and gave the courts a defined but limited role. What does that sequence show about where authority in the state came to rest?

With the courts, which had the strength to settle the dispute before the troops arrived

options.text: With the legislature, which had already lost its powers by an earlier legal change

options.misconception: turns institutional weakness into a claim of total paralysis

questions.hint: Put the steps in order and ask which of them the constitution could have preceded.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The stages of a European integration project
questions.learningObjective: explain why a common currency came last in the sequence
questions.stem: Six states in western Europe placed one heavy industry under joint administration in the 1950s, in 1957 created a common market among themselves with a single external tariff, and only in 1993 created a political union, with a shared currency to follow later still. Which feature of that sequence explains the currency's position?

options.text: A currency required the common market to exist first, since members had to surrender monetary policy
The six states could not agree on a capital for the political union's institutions
options.misconception: invents a disagreement over a capital city to explain the delay

options.text: A single external tariff made a common currency unnecessary for trade to grow
options.misconception: claims a trade measure made money unnecessary for trade

options.text: The political union was attempted first and abandoned before the common market
options.misconception: reverses the order of the stages the sequence records

That sequencing is a checkable feature of the order itself. The distractors supply a disagreement about a capital, an economic claim that does not hold, and a reversed chronology.
questions.hint: Ask what a government gives up when it joins a currency, and whether that could come first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the European project
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a regional integration project
questions.stem: Six states in western Europe built an economic and political union across four decades, changing their treaty framework several times. Put these four developments in the order in which they happened.

One heavy industry was placed under joint administration by the members themselves
A shared currency was created for a group of members that had already agreed to it
A political union was created with common institutions for policy outside the members

questions.hint: Ask which step gave members the practice and trust needed for the next one.

questions.topic: A competence held only at the common level

questions.stem: In the European project, one body alone may propose changes to the treaties, must be consulted on national measures for carrying them out, and is the only negotiator for trade with states outside the group. Which feature best explains why no member's government can run its own external trade policy?

options.misconception: invents a judgment that voided the arrangement for some members

questions.topic: A clause on external trade
questions.learningObjective: read a competence clause for what it forbids members from doing

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The bargain at a tariff round
questions.learningObjective: analyse why tariff reduction meets resistance from import-competing firms
questions.stem: At a long trade round, delegations that had applied high duties on industrial goods agreed to cut them substantially over a period, and in return secured protections for agricultural exporters and promises of wider access for developing countries. Which feature of that bargain does the most to explain resistance at home?

options.text: The cut applied to imports, so the domestic producers of the same goods lost their edge
The cut applied only to raw materials, leaving finished goods protected
options.misconception: restricts the agreement to part of the tariff schedule

options.text: Governments promised a direct payment to every firm that lost ground
options.misconception: invents a compensation scheme that the round did not create

options.text: The round was advisory only, so no national tariff schedule was changed
options.misconception: denies that a binding schedule was actually negotiated

questions.explanation: A tariff is a price wedge that favours the domestic producer of the taxed good, so a schedule that lowers it removes that advantage directly, which is why the loudest resistance comes from the firms whose prices had depended on it rather than from the state as a whole. The distractors shrink the agreement to raw materials, invent a compensation payment, or deny that any schedule changed at all.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the duty change moves in, and who was relying on it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Consequences of removing a tariff
questions.learningObjective: identify the direct consequences of a tariff reduction
questions.stem: A country removes the import tariff on a manufactured good, so buyers of the imported article now face the foreign seller's price without the duty, and domestic firms making a similar article must meet that price. Which changes follow directly from that change? Select all that apply.

options.text: Buyers of the imported article pay less for it than they did while the duty applied
Firms making the domestic equivalent lose the price advantage the duty had given them
The government must replace the lost duty revenue with a new tax of equal size
options.misconception: assumes a replacement tax is required, which the change does not demand

options.text: Buyers of the domestically made article now pay less for it than before
options.misconception: reverses which side of the market gains from a duty cut

The other two either insert a policy consequence, a required replacement tax, that the change does not itself produce, or attach the gain to the wrong side of the market.
questions.hint: Ask which prices actually move, and who competes at the new lower one.

questions.topic: A supply chain that creates dependency
questions.learningObjective: explain how sourcing choices create operational dependency
questions.stem: A firm making a finished product has designed its machinery around one component supplied by a single overseas producer, holds about two weeks of stock, and has never tested an alternative supplier. Which feature of that arrangement does the most to create dependency?

Importing a part legally prevents the firm from exporting its finished goods

options.misconception: invents a treaty rule about how many suppliers a firm may use

questions.topic: A line that stops
questions.learningObjective: analyse a supply failure to identify the binding constraint
questions.stem: In one country a car plant assembles a model whose main electrical component is imported from a single producer two countries away, and parts arrive daily. The plant had declared the component's origin incorrectly to customs officials

questions.topic: Who gains inside one country
questions.learningObjective: identify which groups gain and lose from liberalisation
questions.stem: A country cuts its import tariffs, and within a year its export sector is growing faster than before while the industry that used to compete with imports has lost market share. Which statement about who gains inside that country follows from the change?

options.text: Export workers and buyers of imports gain while the protected industry loses
Every household gains, since cheaper goods must outweigh the losses elsewhere
options.misconception: assumes the gain is spread evenly across all households

options.text: Only foreign producers gain, since the country's own exports remain small
options.misconception: ignores the country's own expanding export sector in the record

questions.topic: A review of quotas and votes
questions.learningObjective: analyse a governance reform in a lending institution
questions.stem: At a governance review of a lending institution, member governments agreed to raise the institution's total quotas, to move part of the shares towards members whose share had been small relative to their output, and to increase the flat vote that every member holds. Which feature of that review is the substantive one?

The review stripped small members of voting rights in exchange for the new quotas

questions.topic: Why five states held a blocking power
questions.learningObjective: explain the origin and the effect of a permanent member's blocking power
questions.stem: Explain why the organisation founded in 1945 gave five named states a power to block any substantive decision, and state what that arrangement did to the organisation's ability to act in a dispute involving one of them.

answer.exemplar: The charter's own entry-into-force clause required ratification by the five named states, so they could not be outvoted and had nothing to gain by leaving, and the price they charged was immunity from a decision they could not accept. What the sponsors had asked for was an organisation able to order action against a state that attacked the peace, and that is what was given up. The effect follows mechanically: because a decision required no negative vote by any of the five, a sponsor could stop action by being absent rather than by recording a vote against, so a body that any one of the five could freeze could not enforce the peace against one of them. That is why the organisation could act against an aggressor outside the permanent membership and largely failed inside it, and the same rule explains the pattern of departures from the chamber in later decades.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: From an inherited boundary to a domestic problem
questions.learningObjective: explain how an external act of partition becomes an internal political conflict
questions.stem: Explain how a boundary drawn by outsiders before a territory had a government of its own turned an act of independence into a domestic political problem, and say at which step the trouble actually begins.

answer.exemplar: A boundary drawn on a map is a claim about space rather than about people, and nobody who lives inside it was asked, so the instant a state is created it inherits communities that the line split and communities that it joined to strangers. The trouble does not begin when the line is drawn but when somebody has to govern: a line on a map has no consequences, whereas a line with a tax office, a court and a land registry behind it has a great many. A group divided by the border presses for access to land and to kin on the other side, and a group outnumbered inside its own province presses for a unit of its own, and each becomes a claim the new government must answer with resources and with force. The government then spends its legitimacy holding together what it inherited rather than building anything new, which is the specific route by which an act of decolonisation becomes a source of domestic conflict and, in the sharpest cases, of partition or collapse.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Who gains and loses inside one country
questions.learningObjective: explain the distribution of gains and losses created by a tariff cut
questions.stem: Explain why cutting an import tariff leaves some people in the exporting country better off and others worse off, and name the single price change that produces both results.

answer.exemplar: A duty is a wedge between the foreign price and the domestic price of the same article, so removing it moves the imported article down and leaves the domestic maker to meet that lower price, and one change does the whole work. Everyone who buys the imported article gains, and so does the country's export sector, which can sell more abroad or buy inputs more cheaply, while firms making the article that the duty used to shelter lose the price advantage and the wages that went with it. Because the two effects come from the same price movement, the national total can improve while the distribution is contested, and that is why organised resistance comes from the losing side rather than from consumers. The losses also tend to be geographically concentrated, so a district whose industry is protected can decline while the country's total rises, which is what makes the change a recurring political problem.
